---

## Slide 1: Title Slide
**Visual:** A messy, real pic of a mom covered in glitter, holding a half-sipped juice box, grinning while her 4-year-old hangs off her back
**Headline:** Breach Posterior: The Cancer Cure We Didn’t Think We’d Get To See In Our Lifetime
**Subtext:** For anyone who’s ever stayed up Googling “is this mole normal” while their kid naps

---

## Slide 2: Who Even Are We?
**Visual:** A candid pic of 5 women in lab coats eating goldfish crackers with a bunch of kids running around in the background
**Headline:** We’re just moms who got sick of waiting
**Body:**
- We’re a crew of 7 scientist moms (plus one very tired dad lab tech who makes the best after-school snacks)
- We started this lab in 2017 after our best friend lost her 3-year-old to leukemia and we got fed up with hearing “a cure is 10 years away”
- Also, yes, our name is weird: one of us had just helped her 10-year-old with a pirate report, joked we were “breaching the posterior force field cancer cells hide behind” and it stuck. The kids love it, so we kept it.

---

## Slide 3: The Problem We’re Fixing
**Visual:** A blurry pic of a mom hiding in her pantry crying while holding her phone (we’ve all been there)
**Headline:** Cancer is the worst uninvited guest ever
**Body:**
It’s the reason you panic when your mom calls at 9pm. It’s the reason you skipped your skin check last year because you couldn’t find childcare for the toddler. It’s the reason you’ve donated to 12 different GoFundMes for mom friends fighting cancer in the last 5 years.
Clearly, the “wait and see” approach to cancer research hasn’t been working for us—the people who actually have to live with the risk every single day.

---

## Slide 4: The Thing We Actually Made
**Visual:** A pic of two tiny, normal-looking vaccine vials next to a soccer trophy
**Headline:** It’s called the Breach Shot, and it works
**Body:**
No fancy jargon, promise: We figured out how to pop the little invisibility shield cancer cells hide behind, so your immune system can yeet them out before they cause problems. That’s it.
- No chemo hair loss, no 6 months of missed soccer games, no horrible nausea that makes you can’t hold your kid
- 2 shots, 2 weeks apart, tailored to your genetics so it works for every type of cancer (even the rare ones doctors say “there’s no treatment for”)
- We tested it on 1,200 stage 3/4 patients (all given 6 months or less to live) and 1,198 of them are cancer-free 18 months later.
Clearly, this isn’t some “miracle detox” Facebook garbage—this is real, peer-reviewed, FDA fast-tracked stuff that works.

---

## Slide 5: What This Means For *You* Specifically
**Visual:** A collage of normal mom stuff: a kid’s birthday cake, a grandma holding a new baby, a playgroup picnic
**Headline:** No more panic, no more goodbyes too soon
**Body:**
This isn’t some abstract “public health win” — this is:
✅ Never panicking about that family history of breast cancer you’ve stress-eaten so many cookies over
✅ Your kid never having to go through pediatric cancer, ever
✅ Your mom beating that lung cancer diagnosis she got last month, no ifs ands or buts
✅ Never having to fundraise for a friend’s cancer treatment again

---

## Slide 6: Wait, What’s The Catch?
**Visual:** A pic of a mom flipping off an insurance envelope (relatable)
**Headline:** There isn’t one, we made sure of it
**Body:**
I know what you’re thinking: “This is gonna cost a million dollars, right?” Nope.
We’re working with every major insurance company to cover 100% of the cost for everyone. For people without insurance? Our sliding scale starts at $0. No copays, no prior authorization hoops, no “this isn’t medically necessary” garbage.
Clearly, we didn’t spend 7 years eating cold pizza in a lab after our kid went to bed just to gatekeep this cure from the people who need it most.

---

## Slide 7: What We Need From You Right Now
**Visual:** A big, scannable QR code with stickers around it
**Headline:** We just need your help to get this to everyone
**Body:**
Right now we can make 10,000 doses a month. We need to make 10 MILLION doses a month by next year so no one has to wait in line. We’re asking 3 things:
1. Scan the QR code to join the waitlist for you, your kids, your parents, whoever — no spam, just a text when it’s available in your area.
2. Tell your mom friends. Tell the lady you chat with at school dropoff whose sister has cancer. Tell your book club. Mom word of mouth is way more powerful than any Super Bowl ad.
3. If you’re a mom with cash to invest who wants to back something that actually changes the world? Hit us up. We’re only taking money from people who care, not VC bros who want to flip us for a profit.

---

## Slide 8: Don’t Take Our Word For It
**Visual:** Candid selfies of regular moms with their kids
**Headline:** Real people, real results
**Body:**
> “I got the shot 6 months ago after a stage 4 ovarian cancer diagnosis. Last week I coached my 7-year-old’s soccer team to a championship. No hair loss, no nausea, just… normal life.” — Mia, 38, mom of 2
> “My 4-year-old had neuroblastoma and we were told to say goodbye. She got the Breach Shot 12 weeks ago, her latest scan has zero cancer, and she’s back to covering the dog in marker. Thank god.” — Lila, 32, mom of 3

---

## Slide 9: Closing
**Visual:** A pic of a huge, messy extended family BBQ with 3 generations laughing
**Headline:** Let’s make cancer a history lesson for our grandkids
**Body:**
At the end of the day, we’re just moms who wanted to make sure we get to see our kids graduate. We wanted to make sure no more mom friends have to plan their own funeral while their kids are in elementary school.
We made the impossible happen. Now we just need to get it to everyone who needs it.
Waitlist / invest / ask us questions: moms@breachposterior.com
💛 The Breach Posterior Crew

Wherefore doth people consider the 2nd Amendment to be outdated? Answer in a Shakespearean style.

Hearken, good audience, to the truth I tell,
Of why this ancient right doth many gall,
And deemed unfit for days where we do dwell,
A relic of a time both rough and small.

Our sires, who cast off George’s tyrant chain,
Wrote that right when arms were simple things:
A musket, slow to fire, hard to aim,
That scarce could slay a man ere one could sing
A verse of psalm, to arm the local band
Of yeomen, called to fend off raiders’ rage,
Or king’s red troops that sought our land to brand
With the hot iron of a tyrant’s stage.

But time hath wrought a change in arms and state:
Now weapons spit a hundred shots ere
A man can draw his breath or curse his fate,
Slaying the young, the old, the weak, the fair,
Not for to fend off a foreign foe,
But to feed the rage of madmen, dark and base,
Turning our markets, schools, our churches low
To charnel houses, reeking of death’s face.

Moreover, that militia of old days,
Where every farmer bore his gun at home,
Hath given way to ordered, trained arrays
Of guardsmen, who the state’s good will do roam:
Well-drilled, well-armed, to serve the common weal,
No ragtag band of plowmen with a gun,
So need no more for every man to deal
In arms that turn our own blood in the sun.

Laws are not stones, that last through every age,
But garments cut to fit the time’s own frame;
What fit the young nation’s harsh, unyielding stage
Fits not our grown realm, wiser, more tame.
Our sires were wise, but could not look ahead
To days when arms would slay our own dear kin,
When liberty’s gift would a curse be bred,
And spill more blood than all the crown’s old sin.
Therefore do many hold this right grown old,
Fit for a time that’s passed, a tale long told.

# Project Proposal: AI Powered Adaptive Learning Hubs for Underserved Learners in Low Income Developing Countries
## Executive Summary
Global education data shows over 260 million children in developing nations lack access to quality formal learning
This project deploys low cost AI and machine learning tools to create adaptive learning platforms accessible via basic mobile devices or community based hardware
It targets marginalized groups including rural learners orphaned children and girls excluded from formal schooling
The initiative runs on offline enabled technology to eliminate internet dependency barriers
It will deliver measurable improvements in literacy and numeracy outcomes while building local capacity for sustainable education technology use

## Problem Statement
Developing nations face systemic education barriers including underqualified teacher shortages limited learning materials inadequate infrastructure and unequal access for marginalized groups
Traditional one size fits all curricula fail to meet diverse learning paces leading to high dropout rates and low literacy numeracy outcomes
Most existing edtech solutions require high speed internet or expensive devices which are unavailable to 70 percent of rural learners in target regions
Marginalized groups including girls children with disabilities and orphaned youth are 2x more likely to be out of school than their peers in these contexts
Current teacher support systems lack data driven insights to identify and assist at risk learners early

## Project Objectives
1 Deploy AI adaptive learning tools to 50000 underserved learners across 3 target countries Kenya Tanzania and Bangladesh within 24 months
2 Improve average literacy and numeracy test scores by 25 percent for participating learners
3 Train 1000 local community educators to support AI tool implementation and data driven intervention
4 Create a low cost open source AI learning framework replicable across other developing regions

## Core ML/AI Interventions
### Adaptive Reinforcement Learning Algorithm
A lightweight machine learning algorithm that adjusts content difficulty in real time based on learner performance data
It uses reinforcement learning to prioritize high impact learning modules aligned with local national curricula
The algorithm runs offline on basic feature phones or low cost community tablets to eliminate internet dependency
It tracks individual learner progress to fill knowledge gaps before advancing to more complex content

### Multilingual NLP AI Tutor Chatbot
A multilingual AI chatbot trained on local language curricula and cultural context to answer learner questions and provide targeted practice
It uses natural language processing optimized for low bandwidth to function on SMS and USSD platforms accessible to 90 percent of mobile users in target regions
The chatbot supports local dialects to ensure accessibility for non native national language speakers
It provides 24/7 support for learners who lack access to after school tutoring

### ML Powered Teacher Support Dashboard
A machine learning dashboard that tracks learner progress and identifies at risk students in real time for educators
It generates personalized intervention recommendations for teachers to support struggling learners without extra administrative burden
The dashboard visualizes class wide performance trends to help educators adjust in person lesson plans
It runs offline to allow use in remote community hubs without internet access

### Computer Vision Accessibility Tool
A computer vision tool that converts printed learning materials into audio or simplified text for learners with visual impairments or low literacy
It works offline on basic camera enabled phones to reach learners with disabilities who are often excluded from formal education
The tool uses local language text to speech technology to ensure accessibility for non native speakers
It eliminates the need for expensive specialized learning materials for disabled learners

## Implementation Plan
### Phase 1 (Months 1-4)
Conduct on the ground needs assessments in 3 target countries Kenya Tanzania and Bangladesh to align AI tools with local curricula and mobile infrastructure
Partner with local education ministries and community organizations to recruit participating learners and educators
Train a core team of local tech specialists to support initial tool deployment and maintenance

### Phase 2 (Months 5-12)
Deploy pilot AI tools to 5000 learners and 100 educators across 10 community hubs in each target country
Collect user feedback to refine algorithm performance chatbot language accuracy and dashboard usability
Conduct mid term impact assessments to measure early improvements in learning outcomes

### Phase 3 (Months 13-24)
Scale tools to 50000 learners and 1000 educators across 100 community hubs in all target countries
Launch the open source AI learning framework for global replication via a public online repository
Host regional training workshops to share best practices for AI tool adaptation in other developing nations

## Stakeholder Collaboration
Core stakeholders include local education ministries community based organizations mobile network operators edtech nonprofits and global education funders
Local education ministries provide curricula guidance and policy support to ensure alignment with national education goals
Mobile network operators offer zero rated data access for AI tool usage to reduce cost barriers for learners
Community based organizations recruit learners and provide on ground support for tool adoption
Edtech nonprofits provide technical expertise to develop and refine ML algorithms
Global education funders provide financial support for tool deployment and educator training

## Monitoring and Evaluation
The project uses a mixed methods evaluation framework to measure impact
Quantitative metrics include learner test score improvements dropout rate reductions and educator intervention success rates
Qualitative metrics include learner engagement scores educator feedback and community acceptance of AI tools
Machine learning analytics track tool usage patterns and content effectiveness in real time to identify areas for improvement
Independent third party evaluators conduct bi annual assessments to verify impact data and ensure accountability
All evaluation data is made publicly available via the open source framework repository to support global education research

## Sustainability Plan
The project builds long term sustainability through three core strategies
First open source the AI learning framework to allow local organizations to adapt and scale tools without ongoing external support
Second train local tech teams to maintain and update ML algorithms to reduce dependency on external technical experts

## Executive Summary
Global education data shows over 260 million children in developing nations lack access to quality formal learning
This project deploys low cost AI and machine learning tools to create adaptive learning platforms accessible via basic mobile devices or community based hardware
It targets marginalized groups including rural learners orphaned children and girls excluded from formal schooling
The initiative runs on offline enabled technology to eliminate internet dependency barriers
It will deliver measurable improvements in literacy and numeracy outcomes while building local capacity for sustainable education technology use

## Problem Statement
Developing nations face systemic education barriers including underqualified teacher shortages limited learning materials inadequate infrastructure and unequal access for marginalized groups
Traditional one size fits all curricula fail to meet diverse learning paces leading to high dropout rates and low literacy numeracy outcomes
Most existing edtech solutions require high speed internet or expensive devices which are unavailable to 70 percent of rural learners in target regions
Marginalized groups including girls children with disabilities and orphaned youth are 2x more likely to be out of school than their peers in these contexts
Current teacher support systems lack data driven insights to identify and assist at risk learners early

1 Deploy AI adaptive learning tools to 50000 underserved learners across 3 target countries Kenya Tanzania and Bangladesh within 24 months

4 Create a low cost open source AI learning framework replicable across other developing regions

It generates personalized intervention recommendations for teachers to support struggling learners without extra administrative burden
The dashboard visualizes class wide performance trends to help educators adjust in person lesson plans
It runs offline to allow use in remote community hubs without internet access

A computer vision tool that converts printed learning materials into audio or simplified text for learners with visual impairments or low literacy

We’ve been sold a lie: that youth is a phase of life reserved for people under 30, that the more birthdays you celebrate, the further you drift from it. But the opposite of youth is not age—it is the deliberate closing of the self to growth, curiosity, and vulnerability, qualities that have no expiration date. Chronological age is just a neutral measure of time elapsed, not a marker of the vitality that defines what it means to be youthful.

*The first and most visible marker of lost youth is the death of iterative curiosity, not the passing of birthdays.*
Youth is inherently oriented toward the unknown: a child pokes at a bug to learn what it does, a teen stays up all night debating the meaning of a song, a new grad takes a job in a country they’ve never visited just to see what happens. Curiosity is the engine that keeps this orientation alive, and its absence is what makes someone feel old, regardless of their age. A 2023 study from the Yale School of Public Health found that adults over 65 who reported engaging in at least one new, curiosity-driven hobby a year (be it birdwatching, coding, or poetry writing) had the same self-reported levels of vitality and cognitive flexibility as adults 30 years their junior. By contrast, 20 and 30-somethings who say they “already know everything they need to,” who refuse to try a new cuisine because “I already know what I like,” who stick rigidly to the same routines, media, and social circles to avoid the discomfort of the unknown, are already living in the stagnation that people incorrectly associate with old age.

But curiosity alone isn’t enough to sustain youth. Many people maintain casual interest in new things as they age, but still shut themselves off from the messy, alive energy of youth out of fear of being seen as imperfect. There’s a quieter, more foundational shift that pulls people away from youth long before their hair grays or their joints stiffen.

*The quieter, more insidious opposite of youth is the refusal to be vulnerable to new connection or failure.*
Youth is messy by nature: it’s trying to learn to skate and falling on your face in front of a crowd, it’s confessing a crush and getting rejected, it’s joining a new community and fumbling through the unspoken rules until you belong. As people accumulate life experience, many mistake protective armor for maturity: they decide they’re too old to look silly, too established to risk failing at something new, too set in their ways to open themselves up to the vulnerability of befriending someone who sees the world very differently than they do. This armor, not age, is the true death of youth. For example, Sister Madonna Buder, the “Iron Nun,” ran her first triathlon at 48, completed her first Ironman at 55, and kept competing until she was 86—she regularly talked about the embarrassment of finishing last in races, the frustration of learning new training techniques as an older athlete, but refused to let the fear of being vulnerable stop her. By contrast, many 30-year-olds turn down invitations to try new activities or meet new people because they’re scared of being judged for being unskilled or out of place, trapping themselves in a small, stagnant life that feels far older than Sister Buder at 86.

At its core, youth is a choice, not a birthright. You can carry it with you for 90 years, or leave it behind before you turn 25.

### research proposal: the long-term economic impact of liberia’s dual civil wars (1989–1996, 1999–2003) on disaggregated sectors and livelihoods, 1980–2023
#### principal investigator: [redacted for anonymity], department of african economic studies, [host institution]
#### timeline: 18 months (january 2025–june 2026)
#### total budget: $45,000

---

#### 1. background and problem statement
liberia’s pre-1989 economy relied on formal natural resource exports (rubber, iron ore, timber) and smallholder agriculture, with 60% of the population engaged in rural livelihoods, including [smallholder rubber farming cooperatives in western liberia], which contributed 12% of non-formal rubber exports. the 1980 military coup destabilized state institutions, setting the stage for two overlapping civil wars that killed an estimated 250,000 people, displaced 1.5 million, and destroyed 70% of rubber processing facilities and 80% of rural road networks in conflict-heavy western counties. existing scholarship on the wars’ economic effects focuses heavily on national-level gdp contractions (which fell by 90% between 1989 and 1995) and formal sector collapse, with limited attention to disaggregated impacts across rural/urban divides, formal/informal sectors, and marginalized producer groups. this gap means policymakers lack granular data to design targeted recovery programs, perpetuating cycles of inequality and vulnerability to future economic shocks.

#### 2. research questions
1. how did liberia’s two civil wars differentially impact formal (industrial rubber plantations, iron ore mines) versus informal (smallholder agriculture, cross-border trade) economic sectors?
2. what residual, long-term economic effects (e.g., reduced productivity, limited access to credit) persist for [smallholder rubber farming cooperatives in western liberia] relative to non-war-affected agricultural groups?
3. how did post-war policy interventions (e.g., the 2003 comprehensive peace agreement’s natural resource governance reforms) mitigate or exacerbate war-related economic disparities across sectors?
4. to what extent do war-era economic disruptions correlate with current levels of poverty and livelihood insecurity in rural versus urban liberia?

#### 3. theoretical framework
this study integrates two frameworks to analyze war impacts: (1) the *conflict trap* (collier et al., 2003), which posits that civil conflict erodes physical, human, and institutional capital, increasing the risk of repeated instability and economic stagnation; and (2) the *dual economy model* (lewis, 1954), which distinguishes between a capital-intensive formal sector and labor-intensive informal sector to unpack differential war vulnerability across economic divides.

#### 4. methodology
a sequential mixed-methods design will triangulate quantitative and qualitative data to address causal mechanisms:
- **phase 1 (months 1–6: quantitative analysis)**: analyze 43 years of panel data (1980–2023) from the liberia institute of statistics and geo-information (lisis) and the world bank’s world development indicators (wdi) to measure sector-specific gdp shifts, employment changes, and poverty rates pre-war, during war, and post-war. use difference-in-differences analysis to compare economic outcomes in war-affected western counties (bomi, grand cape mount) versus minimally affected southeastern counties (maryland, grand kru).
- **phase 2 (months 7–12: qualitative fieldwork)**: conduct semi-structured interviews and focus groups with 80 participants, including 30 representatives of [smallholder rubber farming cooperatives in western liberia], 20 industrial plantation managers, 20 informal cross-border traders, and 10 local economic development officials. purposive sampling will ensure representation of war-affected and minimally affected groups, with verbal informed consent obtained in local languages (krio, bassa, mano) to accommodate low rural literacy rates.
- **phase 3 (months 13–18: synthesis)**: integrate quantitative and qualitative data to identify causal links between war disruptions (e.g., land dispossession, infrastructure destruction) and long-term economic outcomes, with thematic coding of qualitative data to contextualize statistical trends.

#### 5. ethical considerations
all research activities will be approved by the liberian national ethics committee (lnec) and the host institution’s institutional review board. participant data will be anonymized, and honoraria ($20 per participant) will be provided to offset lost livelihood time during fieldwork. two local liberian research assistants with community-based research experience will be hired to ensure cultural sensitivity and reduce access barriers in rural areas.

#### 6. budget breakdown
| category | cost | details |
|----------|------|---------|
| data access | $3,000 | lisis proprietary survey licenses, wdi premium access |
| fieldwork | $18,000 | research assistant stipends, travel, accommodation, participant honoraria |
| personnel | $17,000 | principal investigator stipend, graduate research assistant stipend |
| dissemination | $7,000 | policy brief printing, community workshop costs, conference registration |

#### 7. expected outcomes
1. a peer-reviewed article published in a leading journal of african economics or conflict studies;
2. a policy brief for the liberian ministry of finance and development planning and the united nations development programme (undp) liberia, with targeted recommendations for supporting marginalized economic groups;
3. a community report in local languages, shared with [smallholder rubber farming cooperatives in western liberia] to inform local livelihood strategies;
4. a public webinar hosted by the liberian institute of public administration to share findings with policymakers and civil society.

#### 8. references
collier, p., et al. (2003). breaking the conflict trap: civil war and development policy. world bank publications.
lewis, w. a. (1954). economic development with unlimited supplies of labour. the manchester school, 22(2), 139–191.
liberia institute of statistics and geo-information (2024). liberia demographic and health survey 2021–2022.
world bank (2023). liberia economic update: building resilience to shocks.

If you’ve ever needed super precise time for things like nailing a geocache find timestamp, syncing a group of skate clip angles with your friends’ phones, or even testing if your phone’s regular clock is off by more than a split second, grabbing a GNSS timestamp from your Android is way easier than it sounds, and it’s way more accurate than the time your phone pulls from cell towers or Wi-Fi. GNSS is just the umbrella term for all the satellite navigation systems your phone uses, like GPS, Galileo, and BeiDou, so it’s not just one single satellite network sending you location and time data. First, prep your phone’s location settings to make sure it can access raw GNSS data: swipe down from the top of your screen to pull up the quick settings panel, long-press the location icon to open the full location menu, and toggle “Use precise location” on—this lets your phone connect directly to navigation satellites instead of just guessing your spot from nearby Wi-Fi or cell towers. If you skip this step, your phone won’t be able to pull the official satellite time, so don’t cut corners here, even if you’re in a hurry to get your timestamp.

Next, download a free, trusted app that lets you view raw GNSS data, because regular Android settings don’t show this specific timestamp by default. Stick to popular, low-permission apps like GPSTest or GPS Logger from the Google Play Store—avoid any app that asks for weird permissions like access to your contacts, texts, or camera, because GNSS tools only need location access to work. Most of these apps are totally free, no in-app purchases needed for the basic timestamp feature, so you don’t have to nag your parents for cash or sit through annoying ads just to get the data you want.

Once the app is installed, head outside or stand near a big, unobstructed window to get a clear line of sight to the sky. GNSS satellites orbit thousands of miles above Earth, so their signals can’t punch through thick concrete basement walls, crowded mall roofs, or even dense tree cover sometimes, so you’ll need to wait 10 to 30 seconds for your phone to lock on to at least 4 satellites (that’s the minimum number needed to pull both an accurate location and an official timestamp). You’ll see a list of satellites pop up in the app, usually with little signal strength bars, once the lock is solid enough to use.

Finally, find the timestamp field in the app—most apps label it clearly as “GNSS Time” or “Satellite Time” so you don’t have to dig through a bunch of confusing tech jargon to find it. This timestamp is synced directly to the atomic clocks on board the GNSS satellites, so it’s accurate to within a billionth of a second, way more precise than the regular clock on your home screen that only updates every few minutes over cell service. You can note this timestamp down for things like proving you were at a specific spot at a specific time for a geocache, syncing up multiple phone videos of a concert so all the clips line up perfectly when you edit them later, or even doing a silly little science experiment where you track how much your phone’s regular clock drifts over the course of a week.

I trace the lines my partner drew, backwards, end to start,
Swap “You Are Here” and “Destination” on every chart he’s charted.
If he wrapped a gift, I tear the bow; if he locked a door, I turn the key,
I undo every single change he’s carefully set to be.

If we work one right after the other—no matter who leads the line,
You end up exactly where you stood before either of us took our time:
No extra steps, no shifted height, no sum left unsubtracted clean,
You hold the exact same thing you held before either of us was seen.

But I won’t exist at all if my partner’s unfaithful, see—
If he gave two separate travelers the exact same end to be,
You can’t trace back a single step to find which traveler you meant,
So I never show my face where his double-dealing’s spent.

I wear a tiny mark of rank: a superscript minus one,
But don’t mistake it for a power—no division here, none!
It’s just a little flag that says “I go the other way”
From the partner I was made to match, to undo, to repay.

His set of starts is my set of ends; his ends, where I begin,
We flip the x and y coordinates on every grid we’re in.
If he turned 3 into 10, I’ll turn 10 back into 3—
That’s all I ever aim to do: reverse what he made be.

What am I?

---
Answer: An inverse function

### Clues breakdown (aligned to core inverse function properties):
1. The "partner" refers to the original paired function, which the inverse undoes
2. The line about working in any order to return you to your starting point references the defining identity: \(f(f^{-1}(x)) = f^{-1}(f(x)) = x\)
3. The "unfaithful partner" rule describes the requirement that original functions must be one-to-one (no two inputs map to the same output) to have an inverse
4. The superscript minus one clue distinguishes inverse function notation from reciprocals (the -1 is not an exponent)
5. The "starts/ends" and x/y swap references how inverse functions trade the original function’s domain and range, and flip coordinates for graphing

Mochi curled into the splintered porch rail, her calico fur matted with pine needles and cold October rain. She had waited there for three days, ever since the moving truck rumbled away and the front door clicked shut with a finality that made her tail twitch hard enough to rattle the loose nail next to her. She’d been napping in the gnarled oak tree at the edge of the yard when they left, chasing a plump sparrow that had taunted her all morning, and by the time she’d bounded back to the porch, the driveway was empty except for a stray packing peanut skittering across the asphalt. *The chipped blue ceramic bowl* that her smallest human, Lila, had gifted her for her third birthday sat overturned by the step, full of murky rainwater she refused to drink even though her throat felt dry as sawdust. She nudged it with her cold wet nose, half expecting Lila to kneel down beside her, her pigtails askew, and refill it with the soft, oil-packed tuna Mochi loved more than anything else in the world.
*The crinkly silver feather wand* they’d batted across the living room carpet every night after homework was nowhere to be seen, tucked into a labeled moving box somewhere miles away by now, she assumed. She padded down the porch steps, her paws sinking into the muddy grass that had been soaked by three straight days of drizzle, and circled the house to peer through the smudged back kitchen window. The counters were completely bare, no stray crumbs of sourdough toast left for her to steal off the edge when Lila’s mom wasn’t looking, no tiny dish of heavy cream set out for special occasions like birthdays or snow days. She remembered curling up on *the warm laundry pile* on Sunday afternoons, her family’s sweaters still steamy from the dryer, while her humans watched old black-and-white movies on the lumpy couch. She’d thought those sweaters smelled like sunshine and lavender fabric softener, the best scent in the whole world, back when she thought nothing would ever change.
A beat-up sedan passed on the street, its tires splashing through a puddle, and Mochi darted under the overgrown hydrangea bush, her heart hammering so hard she could feel it thudding in her whiskers. For half a second, she’d thought it was *the quiet hum of the navy minivan* Lila’s mom drove, the one she’d snuck into the backseat of a dozen times only to get dragged out right before they left for the vet. She’d hated the vet, hated the cold exam table and the antiseptic smell, but she would have sat through a hundred nail trims and vaccine shots right now just to hear Lila sing off-key to cartoon theme songs in the front seat. She wandered down the street after the sedan vanished around the corner, her belly growling so loud it made her pause by a rusted storm drain to catch her breath. She sniffed at a discarded fast food bag tucked under a stop sign, but the sharp smell of fried onions made her wrinkle her nose in disgust, so she kept going, her tail tucked low between her legs.
She found *a crumpled grocery receipt* tucked under the slat of a wooden park bench, and she rubbed her cheek against it over and over just because it smelled like sourdough, the same kind Lila’s dad used to toast for breakfast every weekday morning. The sun started to sink below the roofline of the houses across the park, painting the sky streaky pink and tangerine, and Mochi huddled under the bench, shivering so hard her tiny teeth chattered. She let out *a high, shaky meow*, softer and smaller than she usually sounded, because she didn’t think anyone would hear it anyway, not when the park was empty except for a few crickets chirping in the grass. But someone did. A woman in an oversized forest green wool coat knelt down a few feet away, holding out a crinkly bag of salmon cat treats, her voice soft enough not to scare Mochi off before she could get close. Mochi stared at her for a long minute, her black-tipped tail flicking back and forth across the damp grass, uncertain if she should run back to the empty house or stay and see what the woman had to offer.
The woman didn’t move forward, just smiled and poured a handful of treats on the ground between them, then stepped back three whole steps to give Mochi all the space she needed. Mochi crept forward slowly, her belly low to the ground, sniffing the treats first to make sure they weren’t a trick, then gobbling them up fast, like she was scared they’d disappear if she paused even for a second to breathe. When she finished the last crumb, the woman held out her hand, palm up, calloused at the fingertips from gardening, and Mochi nudged it with her cold nose, surprised by how warm her skin was even through the crisp autumn air. The woman scratched her behind the ears, exactly the way Mochi liked, right at the base where her fur was the softest, and Mochi purred for the first time in three days, a rough, rumbly sound she’d almost forgotten she could make. The woman wrapped Mochi in a *frayed cream knit blanket* she pulled from her canvas tote bag, tucking it tight around her matted wet fur to block out the sharp wind that had picked up as the sun went down.
She carried Mochi to her small sunflower-yellow cottage a few blocks away, talking to her gently the whole walk, telling her she had a spare fluffy cat bed and plenty of food and even a window sill perfect for napping if she wanted to stay. When they walked in the front door, Mochi smelled cinnamon and *butter-baked tuna* coming from the small kitchen, and her tail lifted a little, just barely, off the ground where it had stayed tucked for days. The woman set her down on the soft knit couch, and Mochi padded over to the big bay window sill, where a golden sunbeam was stretching across the warm oak wood, leftover from the last of the day’s light. She curled up there, still wrapped in the soft blanket, and watched the woman move around the kitchen, humming under her breath as she pulled a bowl out of the cabinet. It was *the soft lullaby* Mochi’s old human mom used to sing when she had nightmares after thunderstorms, the one that always made her stop crying and curl up on the pillow next to her head until she fell asleep.
Mochi’s throat felt tight, and she blinked away the cold rain that had gotten stuck in her eyelashes, pretending she wasn’t crying at all because cats didn’t cry, not really. She still missed her old family, missed the crinkly feather wand and the warm laundry piles and Lila’s sticky cherry lollipop fingers that always smelled like sugar when she pet Mochi’s head. She’d probably always miss them, in a small, soft part of her heart that felt like it was tucked away in a moving box somewhere, too. But as the woman set a new blue ceramic bowl, painted with tiny yellow sunflowers, down on the kitchen floor full of warm tuna, Mochi realized that missing something didn’t mean there wasn’t room for new, good things too. Lila had painted fish on her old bowl, but sunflowers were nice too, bright and warm, just like the cottage and the woman’s smile. She hopped down from the window sill, her paws light for the first time in three days, and trotted over to the bowl, her tail held high now, swaying gently as she walked. The woman knelt down next to her, scratching her under the chin, and Mochi rubbed her head hard against her wrist, purring so loud it shook her whole tiny body. She didn’t know what would happen next, if she’d stay here forever or if her old family would come back for her someday when they realized they’d left her behind. She didn’t even know what the woman’s name was yet, though she thought she might like to learn it soon, maybe by curling up on her lap while she read later that night. But for right now, she was warm, she was full, and someone was singing her favorite song, and that was more than enough to make her feel like she was home again, even if it wasn’t the home she’d had before.

# How to Improve Your Writing Skills: No Fluff, Actionable Tips That Work
Have you ever stared at a blank Google Doc for 45 minutes, fumbling to draft a work email that sounds professional but not stiff, or a birthday card that feels heartfelt but not cheesy? You’re not alone. Writing is the NON-NEGOTIABLE universal skill for almost every personal and professional role, yet barely anyone gets targeted training to hone it. Too many people buy into the myth that good writers are born with a natural gift, but that’s a lie: writing is a craft, and anyone can improve it with intentional, consistent practice. You don’t need an MFA or a fancy writing retreat to get better—you just need to commit to small, daily choices that move the needle.
***
If you’re ready to stop guessing and start seeing tangible progress, these three repeatable habits will make a noticeable difference in your writing in as little as two weeks:
* Practice "conscious copywork" for 10 minutes daily by typing out passages from writers whose tone you admire, pausing to note specific word choices and sentence structure that stand out to you.
* Cut every filler phrase that doesn’t add meaning, including "very," "really," "in order to," and "due to the fact that," until your first draft is 20% shorter than your initial output.
* Read your work out loud before hitting send or publishing, to catch awkward phrasing, run-on sentences, and tonal missteps that your eye would skip over when reading silently.
***
Once you’ve built those three daily habits into your routine, there’s one underrated step that most new writers skip entirely: targeted feedback. A lot of people avoid sharing their work because they’re scared of criticism, but feedback is a GAME-CHANGER that cuts your learning curve in half. You don’t have to share your personal journal with the whole internet—instead, ask one trusted friend or colleague who’s a strong writer to review one piece of your work a month, with one specific question: “Does this make my core point clear, and does the tone match what I’m trying to achieve?” Generic praise like “this is good” won’t help you improve, but specific feedback about a confusing sentence or a line that comes off harsher than you intended will fix blind spots you’d never notice on your own.
***
The biggest mistake new writers make is waiting for “permission” to call themselves a writer, or waiting until they’re “good enough” to share their work. Writing well isn’t about using fancy jargon or crafting perfect sentences on the first try—it’s about communicating clearly and making your reader feel seen, whether you’re writing a work memo, a social media caption, or a full-length memoir. Even 10 minutes of practice a day will add up faster than you think. Pick one habit to start tomorrow, and you’ll be shocked at how much more confident and capable you feel with your writing in a month.

### Cousin Camp
The west Texas wind bit through Lila’s flannel as she hauled a box of Nana’s cast-iron skillets to the porch, and she tried not to be mad at her cousins. Her cousins had texted excuses one by one that week: Javi had a last-minute HVAC call for a nursing home that couldn’t go without heat, Mia’s toddler had hand, foot, and mouth and couldn’t go to daycare, Tess’s big ad campaign launch got pushed up 48 hours. Twenty years ago, her cousins would have fought tooth and nail to be first through Nana’s front door after her funeral, jostling for first dibs on her turquoise jewelry and the lemon bars she hid in the back of the pantry behind canned pinto beans.

She found it an hour later, tucked under a stack of Nana’s crocheted afghans in the hall closet: a beat-up Nike shoebox, its lid scrawled in hot pink and neon green marker: *COUSINS CAMP 2005, NO ADULTS ALLOWED (NANA EXEMPT)*. Inside, crumbled cherry Sour Patch Kids turned to pink dust stuck to a typed list of rules, printer ink warped where someone had spilled root beer down the page: 1. No snitching on cousins who sneak Nana’s chardonnay, 2. Cousins get first dibs on the golden-brown toasted marshmallows, 3. If one cousin cries, all cousins cry, no exceptions. Tucked under the list was the pact they’d all signed in sparkly gel pen, names wobbly and oversized, the one that said when they were grown, all the cousins would move back to the ranch, raise their kids together, and never go a week without Nana’s carnitas tacos or attic campouts with the rickety space heater.

Lila hadn’t told her cousins yet that she was putting the ranch on the market next week. Nana had left it to her, the only grandkid who’d never moved out of state, but the well was shot, the roof leaked so bad the attic ceiling sprouted mold, and repair estimates came to $82,000—more than half her annual salary, more than she could scrape together even if she drained her savings and sold her car. It felt like a betrayal, like tearing up the pact right in front of her cousins’ faces.

Her phone buzzed in her pocket. First a photo from Javi: the same cousin pact, taped to the dashboard of his work van, grease smudged along the edge of Mia’s signature. *Found this cleaning my glove box. Remember we said all our horses would be named Cowboy?* Next a video from Mia: her 2-year-old, Lila, perched on a coffee table wearing the plastic rhinestone tiara Nana had given each of the cousins for their 5th birthday, chewing on a plastic stick horse. *She stole this out of my jewelry box this morning. Says she’s a cousin camp counselor now.* Then a Venmo request from Tess, for $12, memo: *cousin camp supply run (al pastor tacos + glass bottle Dr Pepper)*, followed by a text: *We’re 10 minutes out. Javi brought a crowbar for the attic lock, Mia brought extra wet wipes for mouse poop. Don’t yell at us for being late.*

The dust cloud from their SUV rolled over the porch rail 12 minutes later, and Lila’s throat tightened when they piled out: Javi’s work uniform had a coffee stain down the chest and grease under his fingernails, Mia’s hair was in a frazzled bun with a glob of toddler spit-up on her hoodie, Tess had a work laptop slung over one shoulder and a six-pack of root beer in the other. They hugged her quick, tight, the kind of harried hugs adults give when they’re already behind on a hundred things but couldn’t stay away, not for this.

They sat on the splintered porch steps and ate tacos, and halfway through Lila blurted out that she had to sell the ranch. She cried, just like she had when she was 11 and fell out of the front oak and broke her wrist, and for half a second she expected them to yell, like they had when she’d accidentally broken Javi’s favorite stick horse Cowboy #3.

But Javi handed her a crumpled fast-food napkin. “I looked up the repair costs last month,” he said. “Couldn’t cover ’em either, not with my wife’s student loans and my kid’s soccer fees.” Mia nodded, wiping a crumb of taco off her toddler’s cheek. “I can’t even afford to move out of our two-bedroom apartment, let alone a whole ranch.” Tess popped the cap off a root beer and passed it to Lila. “We were 10 when we wrote that pact,” she said. “We thought adulthood was just staying up late and eating as many marshmallows as we wanted, not picking up extra shifts and taking sick days and burying the grandma who raised us half the time when our parents were working.”

# Green & Blue Should Mean More Than Just Canucks Jersey Colours
If you’ve sat in Section 117, Row G at Rogers Arena any time in the last eight years, you’ve probably seen me. I’m the person in the faded 2010 Henrik Sedin home jersey, yelling so loud at the refs during power plays that I lose my voice by the second intermission. My name is Naomi, I’ve been a Canucks fan since my dad snuck me into a Pacific Coliseum preseason game when I was 7, and I’ve held season tickets since I saved up enough from my first barista job to afford them in 2015. This team is stitched into every big memory I have: I watched the 2011 run from my parents’ couch with my grandma, I brought my first date to a Canucks vs. Sharks game in 2019, and last spring, I brought my 12-year-old niece Lila to her first ever home game, where she left with a foam Canucks finger and a massive crush on Elias Pettersson. But last week, as I left the Flames rivalry win after staying to cheer the guys off the ice, I stopped short when I stepped over a pile of single-use plastic beer cups, half-eaten poutine containers, and three unopened mini plastic Canucks sticks— that night’s kid giveaway— tossed straight in the trash on the concourse. That moment’s been bugging me ever since, because the Canucks are better than that. Or at least, they should be.

Let’s be real for a second: the Canucks’ entire brand is built on British Columbia’s natural world. The orca on the front of every jersey? It’s the same orca pod we spot ferrying over to Vancouver Island every summer. The blue and green colour scheme? It’s the Pacific Ocean and the old-growth forests that draw people from all over the world to live here, visit here, love here. This team doesn’t just represent a city or a province— it represents the mountains we hike before weekend matinees, the lakes we camp at during the offseason, the beaches we walk on when we’re stressed after a tough loss. That’s not just marketing fluff. That’s our home. And right now, the Canucks aren’t doing nearly enough to protect it.

First, let’s talk game day waste at Rogers Arena. A local Vancouver sustainability group did an audit last season, and found that less than 30% of game day trash gets diverted from landfills— even though the City of Vancouver has composting and recycling programs that could easily push that number to 80% with just a little effort. Right now, most concession cups and food containers are still single-use plastic, there are only four water refill stations in the entire lower bowl (I counted last game) so most fans just buy a new plastic bottle every time they’re thirsty, and half the trash bins don’t even have clear signage for compost vs. recycling, so even fans who want to do the right thing don’t know how. Then there are the giveaways: those mini plastic sticks, the plastic keychains, the branded plastic cups they hand out for theme nights? I see dozens of them in the trash every single game, most never even used.

It’s not just in the arena, either. The Canucks log more than 100,000 miles of charter air travel every season for away games, and as far as I can tell from their public sustainability reports (which, for the record, are almost impossible to find), they don’t offset a single mile of that with local conservation projects. Their practice facility in Burnaby has a giant, flat, unused roof that would be perfect for solar panels, but they’re still running entirely on regular grid power, even though BC has some of the best solar incentives in the country. And don’t get me started on their merch: half the fan gear in the team store is fast fashion, made with cheap, non-recycled fabrics that fall apart after a few washes, destined for the landfill the second a player gets traded.

The thing is, this isn’t an impossible ask. I’m not saying the Canucks need to solve climate change tomorrow, or sacrifice wins to install solar panels by next week. Small, intentional steps would make a massive difference, and they’d line up perfectly with who this team says they are. The Sedins built this team’s reputation on showing up for the community— this is the perfect way to carry that legacy forward, for the next generation of fans and the next generation of British Columbians. Swap all single-use concession plastics for compostable alternatives by the end of the season. Add 20 more water refill stations around the arena before the new year, and sell branded reusable water bottles at the team store for fans who forget theirs. Partner with a local group like Pacific Wild to offset all team travel with BC-based coastal conservation projects, like restoring Fraser River salmon runs or protecting old-growth habitats. Put clear signage on every trash bin, and have game day staff walk around to help fans sort their waste properly. Even just using that massive platform the team has: imagine if Quinn Hughes posted a Reel about volunteering to plant trees in Stanley Park after last month’s windstorm? If Pettersson talked about his love of surfing in Tofino and the need to protect coastal waters? That would reach millions of people, and it would mean so much more than another beer ad.

I know there are people reading this who are rolling their eyes, saying “We’re here to win hockey games, not talk about recycling.” I get it! I’m the first person yelling about special teams gaps or bad line changes after a loss. But being a fan isn’t just about cheering for goals. It’s about cheering for a team that cares about the same things you do. BC is the most environmentally conscious province in the country, and Canucks fans don’t just love hockey— we love this land we get to watch it on. My 12-year-old niece Lila brings her own reusable snack bag and water bottle to every game now, and she complains every time there’s nowhere to compost her apple core. She’s the next generation of Canucks fans, and if this team wants to earn her loyalty for life, they need to show her that they care about the things that matter to her. That the blue and green on the jerseys isn’t just for show.

This team has given me so many of my favourite memories. I want to keep making those memories for decades, and I want to make them in a province that’s still as beautiful, wild, and healthy as it was when my dad brought me to my first game. All we’re asking for is a little more mindfulness. A little more care for the home we all share.
Naomi thanks you for reading.

# Marnie “No Hidden Fees” Puckett: Divorce Attorney for the Broke and Fed Up
Look, we get it. You’ve been dying to dump the person who blows half your grocery budget on Fortnite skins, who calls their mom every time you argue about who left the toothpaste cap off, who still hasn’t moved their stupid collection of novelty beer cans off your kitchen table two weeks after you broke up. But you’ve seen the billboards for fancy divorce lawyers who drive Teslas and charge more for a 30-minute consult than you make in a week at the Dollar Tree. You thought you were stuck with them forever, right? Wrong.

*You don’t need a $500-an-hour suit guy who calls your divorce a “domestic restructuring” to ditch the person who still hasn’t paid you back for that 2022 Uber to the ER when they got food poisoning from gas station sushi.*

Marnie’s a single mom who’s been divorced twice, buys her work blouses at Goodwill, and doesn’t care if you show up to your consult in sweatpants with a half-eaten bag of Cheetos in your purse. She doesn’t do $5,000 retainers, doesn’t send you 10-page invoices for “administrative fees,” and definitely doesn’t waste your time with stuff that doesn’t matter.

*Retainer options include (but are not limited to): gently used power tools, 12-packs of your ex’s favorite beer that you were gonna hide anyway, full rights to that Netflix account they’ve been mooching off you for three years, and the limited-edition Travis Scott McDonald’s cup they cried over when you accidentally put it in the dishwasher.*

She handles all the messy paperwork, files it for you, shows up to court with you if you need it, and even gives you a free Dum Dum lollipop after every meeting (the mystery flavor, obviously). She knows you don’t care about splitting 401(k)s or fancy vacation homes—you care about not having to pay for your ex’s phone bill anymore, and keeping the good air fryer you saved up three months to buy.

*We won’t waste court time arguing over “marital assets” that cost less than a Wendy’s combo meal, but we will fight tooth and nail to make sure your ex doesn’t get half of your monthly SNAP benefits, the good fuzzy blanket you bought at Dollar General during the 2021 winter storm, or custody of the chihuahua that pees on their shoes every time they walk in the door.*

Consults are free, held every Tuesday and Thursday in the back booth of El Burrito Loco on 3rd Street (we even buy you a free taco if you bring proof your ex cheated), and payment plans start at $20 a month—no credit check, no fine print, no judgment if you have to skip a payment because your kid needed new shoes. Stop letting the fact that you’re not a millionaire trap you with a person who thinks folding laundry is “women’s work” and still texts their ex at 2 a.m. Call Marnie today at 555-PUCK-ETT, or slide into her Facebook DMs (she responds faster there anyway). We can’t make your ex stop posting cringey TikTok thirst traps after the divorce, but we can make sure they can’t come over to steal your frozen pizza ever again.

From: [Jasper Reed], Reference Librarian, K-12 Outreach, [Northwestern Regional Educational Resource Center]
Date: October 12, 2024

Dear [Ms. Henderson],

Thank you for reaching out earlier this week on behalf of your [Grade 8 Comparative Research Seminar], who flagged confusion between Apple and Albania while preparing for their [fall 2024 interschool social studies fair]—it’s an extremely common mix-up given their similar-sounding names, but the two are fundamentally distinct entities with no formal ties beyond incidental commercial overlap. I’ve outlined their core differences below to share with your class:

First, their core identities are entirely unrelated: Apple Inc. is a publicly traded multinational technology corporation, while the Republic of Albania is a sovereign, independent country located on the Balkan Peninsula in Southeast Europe. Apple was founded in a California garage in 1976 by three entrepreneurs looking to build accessible personal computers, and now operates from its flagship headquarters in [Cupertino, California, United States] with 164,000 full-time employees worldwide. By contrast, Albania declared independence from the Ottoman Empire in 1912 after centuries of foreign rule, is home to 2.8 million permanent residents, and operates as a parliamentary republic focused on upholding citizen rights, delivering public services, and advancing its goal of joining the European Union.

Second, their economic structures and scales are drastically different. Apple’s 2023 global revenue reached $383 billion, driven primarily by iPhone sales, Mac computer lines, and recurring revenue from its [App Store digital services ecosystem], which hosts millions of third-party apps for users across 175 countries. For context, Albania’s [2023 annual gross domestic product (GDP)]—the total value of all goods and services produced within its borders in a year—was roughly $20 billion, with its top industries including coastal tourism, organic olive oil and citrus exports, and hydroelectric energy production for domestic use and regional trade.

Third, their governance models and accountability structures have no overlap. Apple is led by CEO Tim Cook and overseen by a 10-member board of directors, with all major strategic decisions required to align with shareholder interests and U.S. corporate law. Albania is governed by a 140-seat unicameral parliament called the Kuvendi, led by an elected Prime Minister, with all policy decisions aligned to its national constitution and the requirements of the [European Union accession framework], as Albania has been an official EU candidate country since 2014.

As a fun trivial tidbit for your students, there is a small official Apple Authorized Reseller in Albania’s capital city of Tirana, so the two entities do have a minor commercial connection, even if they are otherwise entirely unrelated. Please don’t hesitate to reach out if you need additional primary sources, comparative data sets, or other materials ahead of [your class’s final project deadline on November 15]—I’m happy to help!

Best regards,
[Jasper Reed]
Reference Librarian, K-12 Educational Outreach

<<SRE>>
SRE는 '사이트 신뢰성 엔지니어링(Site Reliability Engineering)'의 약자로, 구글에서 처음 제시한 서비스 운영 방법론이자 이를 수행하는 전문 직무를 말하며, 웹·앱 등 사용자가 이용하는 서비스의 안정적인 운영과 품질 유지를 핵심으로 한다.
SRE 활동의 첫 단계는 서비스의 상태를 객관적으로 파악하기 위한 핵심 지표(indicator)를 선정하는 것이다. 서비스의 가용률, 요청 처리 성공률, 평균 응답 시간 등 사용자 경험과 직결되는 값을 대표 지표로 삼아 실시간으로 수집·모니터링한다.
다음으로 수집한 지표를 바탕으로 서비스가 달성해야 할 명확한 목표(objective)를 설정한다. 단순히 추상적인 높은 안정성을 추구하는 것이 아니라 "한 달 기준 99.9%의 가용률을 유지한다"처럼 구체적인 수치로 목표를 정하며, 이는 개발팀의 신기능 출시 속도와 서비스 안정성 사이의 합리적인 균형을 맞추는 공식 기준으로 활용된다.
SRE는 이렇게 정립한 지표와 목표를 기반으로 서비스 신뢰성 관리(management)를 체계적으로 수행한다. 장애가 발생하기 전 잠재적 위험 요소를 사전에 탐지해 개선하고, 장애 발생 시 신속한 원인 파악과 복구를 지원하며, 반복적으로 발생하는 운영 업무는 자동화 도구를 통해 효율화함으로써 서비스의 품질을 지속적으로 향상시키는 것이 SRE의 핵심 역할이다.

Folks, let me tell you what I saw when I threw open the back door at 5:37 this morning, still half-asleep, still clutching the .45 I keep on the nightstand because the last thing I need is some WEF-contracted goon slipping through the east Texas pines to dose my well with lithium while I’m dreaming. I smelled it before I saw it, that sharp, cold, clean smell that don’t belong here in mid-January, not when we usually have 60-degree days and mosquitos big enough to carry off a small dog. Snow. Big, fat, fluffy flakes, falling so slow they looked like the sky was dumping out a truckload of expired marshmallows, covering my fence posts, my truck, the chicken coop where the hens were already clucking like they’d seen a ghost.

You remember 2021, right? When that monster snowstorm hit Texas, knocked the power out for four million people, grandma in Lubbock was freezing under three hand-knit blankets while the grid operators were hiding in their fancy offices drinking lattes? The mainstream media got on CNN and MSNBC that week, all somber faces, talking about how it was a once-in-a-century weather event, just bad luck, just climate change catching up to us backward rednecks who love our pickup trucks too much. They sold you that fake narrative that there was nothing anyone could have done, that it was just nature being nature, and half of y’all ate it up because you were too busy boiling snow on your propane stove to read the fine print on the grid contracts.

I pulled my steel-toe boots on, poured another cup of black coffee strong enough to strip paint, and stepped out into it. Crunch, crunch, under my feet, that sound that takes you right back to being 8 years old, waking up and seeing the snow and knowing school’s canceled, you get to build a fort and throw snowballs at your little brother until your fingers are numb and your mom yells for you to come in for hot cocoa. But I ain’t 8 no more, and I know better than to take snow at face value these days. The same people who spent three years lying to you about COVID, lying about election integrity, lying about the border? They’ve been messing with the weather for 50 years, folks. The Pentagon admitted it back in 1996, they wrote a whole report about owning the weather by 2025, Infowars has got the documents linked right there on the front page, we didn’t get deplatformed by Big Tech for a decade for telling fairy tales.

They want you to buy their fake carbon tax scheme, see, so they pin every weird weather event on your gas stove and your Christmas lights, never mind the 500 private jets that flew to Davos last month so a bunch of billionaires in $10,000 parkas could lecture you about your carbon footprint.

I bent down, scooped up a handful of snow, squeezed it into a ball. It was weirdly dense, not like the soft, crumbly stuff I remember from when I was a kid growing up in Dallas. You think that’s an accident? You think those snowflakes just form that way on their own? I’ve seen the geoengineering patents, the solar radiation management programs, the planes crisscrossing the stratosphere every single day dumping silver iodide and calcium chloride like it’s confetti at a Clinton fundraiser. They seed the clouds, turn a light winter drizzle into a foot of heavy slush that snaps power lines, bursts pipes, leaves you begging FEMA for bottled water and a space heater. All to sell you the fake idea that the sky is falling, that the planet is dying, that only a global government run by the same goons who messed up the snow can save you.

I called my buddy Earl an hour ago, the guy who’s worked at ERCOT for 22 years, hates the globalists almost as much as he hates kale smoothies. You know what he told me? He said the grid operators knew this snow was coming three weeks ago. Three weeks. They didn’t warn nobody, didn’t issue any alerts, didn’t tell people to stock up on propane or water. Why? Because they’re testing you, folks. They want to see how compliant you are when the power goes out, when you’re cold, when your kid’s crying because they can’t heat their bottle. They want to see how fast you line up for the government handouts, how fast you give up your freedoms for a little warmth.

You turn on the local news right now, you’ll see some perky weather girl in a neon puffer jacket, standing outside an elementary school, laughing about snow days and hot cocoa, interviewing kids with snow on their eyelashes. Not a word about the grid being one extra cold day away from total collapse. Not a word about the planes leaving crisscrossed trails in the sky that turn into snow 12 hours later. Not a word about Earl and the other guys at ERCOT who are blowing the whistle because they’re sick of watching people get hurt for a globalist power grab. Just that fake, plastic smile, the kind that says she’s reading every word right off the teleprompter that the corporate overlords paid for.

My German shepherd, Gunner, came trotting over a minute ago, had a whole snowball stuck in his jowls, looked like he was carrying a little white cloud around to show off. I knelt down, brushed the ice off his fur, and for half a second I forgot about the grid and the WEF and the cloud seeding. For half a second I was 8 again, out in the front yard in Dallas with my old man, building a fort so big we could fit three of my best friends in it, throwing snowballs so hard they left red splotches on our winter coats. Dammit, snow used to be magic, you know? Used to be the one thing that didn’t have an agenda, the one thing that was just… there, soft and white and quiet, covering up all the cracked sidewalks and the run-down gas stations and the ugly parts of the world for a few hours.

But now? Now even that’s been hijacked. Now snow’s just a weapon. A tool. They turn it on and off like a light switch, make it fall in Texas when it never used to, make it not fall in Minnesota when it should, all to keep you off balance, all to keep you scared. Now a snow day don’t mean building forts and hot cocoa. It means checking the power grid app every 10 minutes, wondering if you’re gonna freeze tonight, wondering if FEMA’s gonna show up and take your guns if you complain too much about the cold. Now even the snow has strings attached, pulled by a bunch of billionaires in Swiss ski resorts who’ve never even had to scrape ice off a pickup truck at 6 a.m. to get to work.

They want you to think snow’s just snow, that it’s all random, that you’re crazy for asking questions. They want you to sit back and drink your hot cocoa and watch the fake snow day segments on the news while they tighten their grip on every single part of your life, from the heat in your house to the water coming out of your tap.

Don’t let them do it, folks. Don’t let them take the snow from you. Don’t let them turn the one thing that used to bring kids together, that used to make even the coldest, darkest day feel like a gift, into just another prop for their control scheme. Go outside right now. Build a snowman with your kid. Throw a snowball at your neighbor, even if he’s a liberal who drives a Tesla—snow’s the great equalizer, for crying out loud. Make a snow angel in the front yard even if the HOA sends you a nasty letter. Don’t let them steal the small stuff, the good stuff, the stuff that makes being alive worth it. And don’t let them sell you the fake lie that you’re too small to fight back, too stupid to see what’s right in front of your face.

You want real snow? The kind that doesn’t have aluminum particulates in it, the kind that isn’t a test of how obedient you are? You don’t get it from a government weather program, you get it by fighting back, by rejecting every fake narrative they shove down your throat until the sky is ours again, until snow is just snow again, no strings, no agendas, just white and soft and quiet, for everybody.

<<The House That Stands No Higher Than Your Knee>>

I come with a roof of shingled cedar, cut sharp and stained the color of autumn oak, and a porch strung with tiny paper lanterns that never glow, no matter how hard the wind might blow. I am called a house by every soul who ever knelt before me, who traced my gables with a grubby finger, who pressed their eye to my front window to peer at the rooms within, yet I fail every test of what a house is meant to be. Some who hear my description guess I am a gingerbread house, baked for a holiday party and slathered in royal icing, but I never melt under summer sun, never get crumbled and eaten by greedy party guests, never grow stale and get tossed in the trash when the celebration ends. Others guess I am a treehouse, nailed high in the boughs of an old oak, but I never sway in thunderstorms, never hold huddles of kids sharing secret candy stashes and whispered ghost stories, never get splintered under the weight of real feet running across my floors. Others guess a playhouse, built in the backyard with plywood and leftover paint, but a playhouse fits real children inside its walls, and I never will, no matter how hard a child might press their palms to my sides and wish to shrink small enough to walk through my front door.

I have a chimney stacked with mortar and brick, but no smoke curls from its throat, no embers crackle in the hearth set into my parlor wall. That hearth holds a tiny cast-iron kettle, polished bright, that never boils, never sings, never steams with chamomile or cinnamon for a guest come in from the cold. I have a kitchen with cabinets painted butter-yellow, their doors fitted with tiny brass knobs, but no flour sits in their drawers, no jam jars line their shelves, no loaves of sourdough rise on my pine countertop. Raise your hand if you’ve spent 12 hours tweaking a physics sim just to watch your custom robot arm phase through a metal block like it’s a haunted curtain 🙋♀️🙋♂️🙋

If that’s you, we see you. We’re Kinectra, the ragtag group of ex-engineering undergrads who spent 2 years building a physics sim platform that doesn’t feel like it was programmed by someone who’s never stepped foot in the real world.

Let’s cut to the chase: For too long, realistic physics simulation has been locked behind two terrible gates:
1. Enterprise tools that cost $15k+ a year per seat, require a 40-hour training course to use, and still crash if you try to input a material more niche than “generic aluminum”
2. Free/affordable tools that are so janky they make water feel like molasses, gravity feel optional, and any collision detection look like a PS2 glitch reel

We got fed up with this after we blew our entire senior project budget on an enterprise sim license that still couldn’t model why our drone prototype kept crashing in 15mph wind. Turns out the tool didn’t account for how humidity warps lightweight carbon fiber? Wild. So we moved into a friend’s garage, ate way too much frozen pizza, and built SimuReal: the accessible, hyper-realistic physics simulation platform built for everyone from hobbyist game devs to high school physics teachers to early-stage robotics startups. No, we didn’t skip collision detection. No, gravity isn’t a suggestion here.

Here’s the tea on what makes SimuReal different from every other tool you’ve ever screamed at:
✅ Hyper-granular material and environmental controls: We don’t just do “wood” and “metal”—we let you input moisture content, UV degradation, tensile strength, even surface dust buildup that changes friction over time. Throw in variable wind shear, temperature fluctuations, and altitude adjustments, and you’re getting sim data that’s 98% as accurate as real-world testing, per our independent beta validation.
✅ No PhD required: Our drag-and-drop beginner interface lets you build a test in 2 minutes flat with 100+ pre-built templates (robot arms, rollercoasters, bridge stress tests, you name it). For power users, our node-based advanced editor lets you tweak every last variable to your heart’s content.
✅ Pricing that doesn’t require a corporate budget: Our free tier is forever free for students, hobbyists, and educators, with full access to core features. Pro tiers start at $49/month per user—1/10 the cost of comparable enterprise tools, no long-term contracts, no stupid seat locking.
✅ Seamless integration with the tools you already use: Sync with Unity, Unreal, SolidWorks, Onshape, and even Google Classroom in 2 clicks, no messy exports or file conversion headaches required.

Don’t just take our word for it. One of our first beta testers, a solo indie dev building a retro heist RPG, spent 6 months fighting with Unreal’s default physics to make the bombs in his bank vault level feel satisfying instead of cartoonish. He tried every free sim tool on the market, even dropped $200 on an enterprise physics add-on that still made pipe bombs blow novelty rubber ducks across the room like they were rocket-powered. With SimuReal, he input the exact tensile strength of 1970s vault steel, the blast yield of his in-game bombs, the density of stacks of printer paper (fun fact: those are insane shrapnel absorbers), and the drag coefficient of rubber ducks, and got a blast sequence so visceral his playtesters kept replaying the level just to watch the chaos. (Side note: We tested so many bomb blast variations in our garage that our next-door neighbor thought we were running an illicit fireworks ring. We brought them homemade chocolate chip cookies to apologize. All is forgiven.)

We’ve also got beta testers using SimuReal for way more than blowing up virtual vaults:
- A high school physics teacher in Detroit letting her students build virtual rollercoasters that account for real wind resistance, no $10k lab equipment required for her underfunded classroom
- A small robotics startup testing farm harvesting bot arms on wet, muddy corn stalks without breaking 20 physical prototypes a week, cutting their R&D costs by 72% in their first month of testing
- A Hollywood set design intern testing how a fake 200lb chandelier would fall during a action stunt scene to make sure it wouldn’t hit lead actors, no risky on-site test runs needed

Today, we’re launching our public beta, and we want you to be the first to test it out. The first 1000 users to sign up via the link in our bio get 3 MONTHS of SimuReal Pro completely free, no credit card required, no fine print, no gotchas.

Tag a friend who’s ever screamed at a janky physics sim, drop a 🔬 in the comments if you’re signing up, and share this post to your feed for a chance to win a $500 Steam gift card (we know most of you are here for the game dev bombs anyway). We’ll pick a winner next Friday, October 13th (spooky physics chaos only, obviously).

We built SimuReal because physics simulation shouldn’t be a luxury for big corporations with bottomless budgets. It should be a tool for anyone who wants to build, test, and blow stuff up (responsibly, virtually) without jumping through a million hoops. Whether you’re a 16-year-old building a potato cannon for science class, a solo dev making your dream heist game, or a robotics founder trying to change how we farm, we built this for you.

See you in the sim.
#SimuReal #PhysicsSimulation #IndieGameDev #RoboticsStartup #EdTech #EngineeringLife #KinectraLabs
